title: Wendell and the Harvest
premise: Odile Lockridge, a hospice nurse who has spent fifteen years rationalizing the backwards counting he hears from the dying, returns to his childhood village of Harrow's Bend when his estranged aunt falls ill. There the church bell—melted down in 1911 after a drowning scandal—begins to ring at dusk, and Odile realizes the counting is not death approaching but something beneath the village well keeping score of an old crime. The drowned children of 1911 were never mourned, only buried in ledgers and lies, and now they are calling their names back. To save his aunt and the makeshift family he has gathered—a deaf gravedigger, a runaway teen, and the last honest descendant of the men who did the drowning—Odile must descend into the refilling well before the count reaches zero and take the village's confession down with him. The ending demands justice outside any court: the truth spoken aloud at the bell's rope, the guilty line ended by choice rather than violence, and Odile finally letting himself be seen.
about_author: Beatrix Montrose is the pen name of a former rural hospice worker who spent a decade collecting the things patients say in their final hours. She writes horror about small communities keeping large secrets, and lives somewhere with a well she refuses to drink from.

chapters.title: The Backwards Count
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. In a city hospice, Odile sits with a dying man who counts down from forty in a voice that isn't quite his own; Odile logs it as terminal lucidity, as always. The beat: weary self-deception established—we see the rituals he uses to stay invisible.

chapters.title: A Letter in Aunt Vera's Hand
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A letter arrives from Harrow's Bend: Aunt Vera is dying and asking for him, though they haven't spoken since he left at nineteen. He tells himself he'll stay a week. Beat: guilt cracking the shell of his carefully managed anonymity.

chapters.title: The Village That Forgot Its Bell
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Arriving by bus, Odile passes the church—roofless since the fire—and remembers the bell was melted down in 1911 for war metal. The village feels watched. Beat: homecoming as quiet dread.

chapters.title: Vera Counts Too
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Bedridden Vera hears her nephew arrive and pretends to sleep; under her breath she counts backwards from thirty-nine. She knows what the counting means and has been waiting fifteen years for someone else to hear it. Beat: dread with tenderness.

chapters.title: The Gravedigger Who Reads Lips
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile meets Tam Osgood, the deaf gravedigger, who communicates in chalk and gestures and knows more village history than anyone alive. Tam warns him, wordlessly, to leave before harvest. Beat: first ally, first warning.

chapters.title: The Bell Rings at Dusk
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. At sunset a single toll rolls over the village—from a church with no bell. Only Odile, Vera, and Tam seem to hear it. Beat: the rationalizations collapse; horror becomes undeniable.

chapters.title: Runaway at the Well House
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile catches sixteen-year-old Junie squatting in the derelict well house, fleeing a foster placement. Instead of turning her in, he feeds her. Beat: the found family begins assembling itself out of strays.

chapters.title: Ledgers of the Drowning Year
chapters.summary: Tam's POV (rendered through written notes). Tam shows Odile parish records from 1911: seven children drowned in the well, blamed on a 'fever,' the bell melted to fund the cover-up. Beat: the historical wound opens.

chapters.title: What the Dying Say
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Vera, lucid, confesses she has heard the counting all her life and that each dying villager counts down the days until 'the well refills.' She asks Odile to listen this time instead of explaining. Beat: permission granted to believe.

chapters.title: Junie Hears It First
chapters.summary: Junie's POV. Junie, sleeping in the well house, wakes to children's voices reciting names she doesn't know. She runs to Odile and, for the first time, someone believes her instantly. Beat: belonging forged in fear.

chapters.title: The Hollis Family Pew
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile visits Edith Hollis, matriarch of the family that owned the mill in 1911, ostensibly about Vera's care. Edith's courtesy has teeth. Beat: the antagonist introduced—polite, immovable, keeper of the lie.

chapters.title: Thirty-Three Days
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Vera's count drops to thirty-three; she rallies enough to draw Odile a map of the old village—seven small crosses around the well. Beat: urgency made visible; love expressed as cartography.

chapters.title: Chalk Marks on Every Door
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Overnight, seven chalk crosses appear on doors across the village—including Edith Hollis's. The villagers scrub them furiously and refuse to discuss them. Beat: collective denial as horror engine.

chapters.title: Edith's Offer
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Edith offers Odile money to take Vera to a city facility and go. She mentions his years of invisibility with unsettling precision. Beat: temptation—the old escape route offered back to him.

chapters.title: The Night the Water Rose
chapters.summary: Junie's POV. Junie watches the dry well begin, impossibly, to seep water. She fills a jar of it; by morning the jar is empty and smells of river mud and pennies. Beat: the countdown acquires a physical clock.

chapters.title: Names in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Cross-referencing records, Odile learns one drowned child was a Hollis by blood—hidden because she was illegitimate. The family didn't just cover up the deaths; one of their own was among the victims. Beat: moral complication deepens.

chapters.title: Tam's Grandfather's Rope
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam inherits his grandfather's toolbox and finds inside a length of bell-rope and a note: 'When it rings true, pull.' Tam doesn't know if it's an instruction or a curse. Beat: inheritance as burden; the tool of climax planted.

chapters.title: Twenty-Six Days
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Vera's count accelerates. Odile stops charting her decline clinically and simply holds her hand while she counts, matching his breathing to hers. Beat: the nurse learns presence over procedure.

chapters.title: The Constable Who Isn't
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile reports the disturbances to the village constable, who turns out to be on Edith's payroll and gently threatens Junie's custody status. Beat: the law revealed as another locked door—justice must come from elsewhere.

chapters.title: Junie Runs, Then Doesn't
chapters.summary: Junie's POV. Terrified, Junie packs to flee but returns when she realizes leaving means Odile and Vera face the count alone. Beat: choice defines family; the found family solidifies.

chapters.title: The Harvest Supper
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Edith hosts the annual harvest supper; attendance is compulsory by custom. Under lantern light, villagers perform normalcy while the bell tolls faintly between courses. Beat: communal complicity staged as celebration.

chapters.title: Vera's Confession
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Vera admits that as a girl she saw the children go into the well and said nothing—her silence bought the family's respectability. She asks not forgiveness but witness. Beat: memory as both wound and key.

chapters.title: Nineteen Days
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile tests the well with a stone on a string; the string comes up frayed and cold, and the depth reading makes no sense. Beat: dread escalates through wrongness of scale.

chapters.title: Edith Breaks
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Alone, Edith reads the 1911 letters her great-grandmother wrote and learns the drownings were no accident—the children were sent down to retrieve a dropped millstone and the ladder was pulled away. Beat: the antagonist's certainty cracks; she becomes tragic.

chapters.title: The Bell Rings Thrice
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs braided. Three tolls shake the village at midnight; every resident wakes remembering a different child's name they'd never learned. Beat: the dead stop whispering and start demanding.

chapters.title: Fifteen Days
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Vera's count hits fifteen. Odile organizes the household—Tam fortifying the well house, Junie copying the ledger, himself drafting the confession no court will ever hear. Beat: purpose replaces paralysis; the plan takes shape.

chapters.title: What Refills the Well
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam deciphers his grandfather's other notes: the well refills every time the village forgets, and drains only when the names are spoken publicly at the rope. Memory is literally structural. Beat: theme crystallized into mechanics.

chapters.title: Edith Comes at Night
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Edith arrives unannounced, not to threaten but to ask what her family owes. Odile tells her: the truth, aloud, at the bell. She leaves without answering. Beat: the antagonist reaches her hinge point.

chapters.title: Eleven Days
chapters.summary: Junie's POV. Junie finishes transcribing the ledger and reads the seven names aloud to the kitchen; the water in the well audibly drops an inch. Hope arrives—but so does the sound of many feet below. Beat: hope and escalation entwined.

chapters.title: The Village Turns
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Edith's cousins, fearing exposure, move against her: the constable serves papers declaring her incompetent. The machinery of the lie devours its keeper. Beat: villainy fracturing; stakes shift from secrecy to succession.

chapters.title: Seven Days
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Vera's count reaches seven. She gives Odile her mother's ring and extracts a promise: whatever happens below, he comes back up with the names spoken. Beat: farewell prepared without farewell said.

chapters.title: The Rope and the Ruin
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam rigs the melted bell's surviving yoke with his grandfather's rope above the open well shaft. Testing it, he hears, faintly, seven voices keeping time like a work song. Beat: the instrument of climax assembled amid rising terror.

chapters.title: Four Days
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The well water rises visibly now, flooding the churchyard. Villagers begin leaving; those who stay gather nightly at Edith's fence, wanting to be told what to do. Beat: the community's hunger for someone to break the silence.

chapters.title: Two Days
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Edith, stripped of standing, comes to the house and says yes—she will speak the names. But the count must reach zero at the well itself, and someone must be there to pull the rope. Beat: the cost named; volunteers weighed.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. With the count at one, Odile goes down the well shaft with the ledger, Junie's lamp, and Vera's ring, while Tam mans the rope and Edith waits at the lip with the names. Beat: climax begins—descent as acceptance.

chapters.title: The Counting Room
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Below the waterline, Odile finds a dry chamber where seven children sit counting, and understands they cannot stop until someone counts with them—backwards to zero, together. He sits down among them. Beat: terror transfigured into communion.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: Braided POVs. As Odile speaks the final number, Edith cries the seven names into the wind and Tam pulls the rope; the melted bell rings one true note. The water drains, the children stand, the count ends. Beat: catharsis—memory performed as rite.

chapters.title: Above Ground
chapters.summary: Junie's POV. Junie hauls Odile up half-drowned; Vera dies peacefully at dawn, her count finished, smiling. The village, unable to unhear the names, begins digging up its real history. Beat: grief braided with release.

chapters.title: The New Bell
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Months later, the village casts a new bell inscribed with seven names, paid for by the dissolved Hollis estate. Odile stays—not hiding now, but choosing. Beat: justice outside the law completed; visibility embraced.

chapters.title: Harvest Again
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. One year on: Odile, Junie, and Tam share the harvest supper at a table that includes Edith, diminished and present. When a dying patient far away counts backwards now, Odile listens—and answers. Beat: resolution; the found family endures, and listening becomes his gift.
